sites.name: Haughton Crater, Devon Island
programs: Haughton-Mars Project (NASA Ames / Mars Institute / SETI Institute)
sites.summary: A ~23 km impact structure in a polar desert (formed ~39–31 million years ago; the age is debated), used since 1997 to study impact geology, periglacial processes and the human and robotic exploration of the Moon and Mars.

similarities.explanation: Well-preserved complex crater with shocked gneiss, impact-melt breccias and impact-generated hydrothermal deposits, comparable to mid-sized Martian craters.
Ice-wedge polygons, gullies and patterned ground in permafrost resemble Martian periglacial landforms.
Continuous permafrost with ground ice close to the surface.
Polar-desert climate with mean annual temperatures around −16 °C.
Fossil impact-induced hydrothermal veins and vugs, a template for impact-driven habitats on Mars.
Reachable only by aircraft; field crews operate with limited logistics and communications.
Rugged, unvegetated terrain used for rover (K10), pressurised-vehicle and simulated EVA traverses.
Impact lithologies and crater structure useful for training crews to recognise impactites.
Remote field base used to rehearse lunar surface operations and medical contingencies.
Used for robotic and simulated lunar EVA operations, including a 2006 lunar medical contingency simulation.

limitations.explanation: Earth's dense atmosphere and magnetic field shield the surface from radiation and micrometeorites; the Martian surface has neither.
Surface gravity is about 2.6 times that of Mars, which changes slope stability, sediment transport and crew workload.
Seasonal liquid water and active streams; the Martian surface is too cold and the air too thin for stable liquid water today.
Microbial life and sparse vegetation are present, unlike any known Martian environment.
The Moon has no permafrost, water ice in the sampled terrain, or periglacial processes; only the impact geology transfers.
Surface gravity is about six times that of the Moon, so suits, rovers and regolith mechanics behave differently.

researchUse: Haughton-Mars Project expeditions (1997–present) on impact geology, astrobiology and exploration technology.
K10 rover field tests and robotic follow-up of human traverses.
2006 NASA lunar medical contingency simulation.
MIT/NASA studies of interplanetary supply-chain logistics (2005).

Shocked Precambrian gneiss from the Haughton impact structure (8.8 cm across).

target.caption: Victoria crater (~750 m), Meridiani Planum, with Opportunity on the rim.
Linné crater (2.2 km), a young, fresh simple crater in mare basalt, Mare Serenitatis.

sites.name: Black Point Lava Flow, San Francisco Volcanic Field
sites.summary: A basaltic lava flow and cinder field north of Flagstaff that has been NASA's main Desert Research and Technology Studies (D-RATS) site for testing pressurised rovers, robots and EVA operations.

similarities.explanation: Basalt flows and cinder resemble the volcanic plains of the lunar maria.
Used for multi-day pressurised-rover missions (2008–2011, 2022) and EVA traverse planning.
Cinder and fine volcanic sand allow mobility testing, though grain shapes and mechanics differ from lunar regolith.
Field geology tools, sampling procedures and science back-room operations tested during D-RATS.

limitations.explanation: Earth's dense atmosphere and magnetic field shield the surface from radiation and micrometeorites; the Moon has neither.
Surface gravity is about six times that of the Moon, so suits, rovers and regolith mechanics behave differently.
Terrestrial fines lack agglutinates, nanophase iron and the sharp, unweathered grains of lunar regolith produced by space weathering.
Desert vegetation, wind and rain-driven erosion are absent on the Moon.
Daylight and thermal cycles differ greatly from the 14-day lunar day and extreme lunar polar lighting.

researchUse: D-RATS 2008: 72-hour crewed test of the Small Pressurized Rover.
D-RATS 2009: Tri-ATHLETE robot and K10 scout rover tests.
D-RATS 2010–2011: integrated multi-destination and asteroid mission simulations.
D-RATS 2022: Artemis-era pressurised rover operations with NASA and JAXA crews.

sites.name: SP Crater, San Francisco Volcanic Field
programs: JETT3 (Artemis EVA & Human Surface Mobility test team)
sites.summary: A symmetrical, ~250 m high basaltic cinder cone with a long lava flow, used in October 2022 for night-time Artemis III moonwalk rehearsals under lighting that mimicked the lunar south pole.

similarities.explanation: Scoria cone and tephra blanket, a terrestrial counterpart to lunar dark mantle (pyroclastic) deposits.
Basaltic andesite lava flow extending ~6 km from the cone.
Used for simulated Artemis EVAs, including low-sun-angle lighting tests.
Astronauts practised describing and sampling volcanic geology during JETT3.

limitations.explanation: Earth's dense atmosphere and magnetic field shield the surface from radiation and micrometeorites; the Moon has neither.
Surface gravity is about six times that of the Moon, so suits, rovers and regolith mechanics behave differently.
Terrestrial fines lack agglutinates, nanophase iron and the sharp, unweathered grains of lunar regolith produced by space weathering.
Lunar pyroclastics are glass beads from fire-fountaining, not cinder cones; lunar cones are rare and small.

researchUse: JETT3 field test (October 2022): night-time Artemis III EVA simulations with flight control and science teams.

sites.name: Meteor Crater (Barringer Crater)
sites.summary: A ~1.2 km, ~50,000-year-old simple impact crater in layered sedimentary rock, one of the best-preserved on Earth and a training site for astronauts since 1963.

similarities.explanation: Simple bowl-shaped crater with overturned rim strata and ejecta, morphologically similar to fresh lunar craters of similar size.
Used for Mercury, Gemini and Apollo crew training and in current NASA astronaut geoscience training.
Rim and ejecta traverses used to practise sampling and description, historically in suits.

limitations.explanation: Earth's dense atmosphere and magnetic field shield the surface from radiation and micrometeorites; the Moon has neither.
Surface gravity is about six times that of the Moon, so suits, rovers and regolith mechanics behave differently.
Target rocks are sandstone and limestone, unlike the basalt and anorthosite of lunar craters.
Erosion and vegetation have modified the crater; lunar craters of this age remain sharp.

researchUse: Astronaut field geology training from 1963 through Apollo 17, and for later astronaut classes.
Impact fracturing and structural studies.

sites.name: Cinder Lake Crater Field
sites.summary: Artificial crater fields blasted by the USGS in 1967–1968 into basaltic cinder to reproduce part of the Apollo 11 landing area; used for Apollo crew training and still used for testing.

similarities.explanation: Explosion craters reproduce the size and spacing of a lunar crater field, but not true impact processes.
Dark basaltic cinder over clay provides a loose, low-albedo surface for traverse practice.
Apollo crews (first used by Apollo 13 in 1970) practised geological traverses here.
Used for rover and suit testing from the Apollo era to the present.

limitations.explanation: Earth's dense atmosphere and magnetic field shield the surface from radiation and micrometeorites; the Moon has neither.
Surface gravity is about six times that of the Moon, so suits, rovers and regolith mechanics behave differently.
Terrestrial fines lack agglutinates, nanophase iron and the sharp, unweathered grains of lunar regolith produced by space weathering.
The craters are explosion features and have degraded since the 1960s; they lack shock metamorphism.

researchUse: Apollo astronaut traverse training (1970s).
USGS drone topographic surveys (2023–2024).
Testing of Artemis-era equipment.

sites.name: Mauna Kea upper flanks (ISRU test sites)
sites.summary: High-altitude volcanic terrain with fine tephra and cinder used in NASA/CSA/DLR field campaigns to demonstrate lunar resource prospecting, excavation and oxygen extraction.

similarities.explanation: Fine-grained basaltic tephra (e.g., at Puʻu Hiwahine) used as a field regolith simulant.
Field demonstrations of regolith excavation, hydrogen reduction, carbothermal oxygen production and Mössbauer prospecting.
Basaltic to hawaiitic cinder cones and lava flows.
RESOLVE prospecting payload and miniaturised Mössbauer spectrometers field-tested.
Resource-processing hardware relevant to Mars surface operations was tested in the same campaigns.
Palagonitic Hawaiian tephra (Puʻu Nene cinder cone, in the saddle south of Mauna Kea) was the source of the JSC Mars-1 soil simulant.
Summit area above 4,000 m has about 60% of sea-level pressure, still more than 100 times Mars' pressure.

limitations.explanation: Earth's dense atmosphere and magnetic field shield the surface from radiation and micrometeorites; the Moon has neither.
Surface gravity is about six times that of the Moon, so suits, rovers and regolith mechanics behave differently.
Terrestrial fines lack agglutinates, nanophase iron and the sharp, unweathered grains of lunar regolith produced by space weathering.
Tephra is altered by water and contains hydrated minerals unlike lunar regolith.
Snow, rain and vegetation are present at lower elevations.
Surface gravity is about 2.6 times that of Mars, which changes slope stability, sediment transport and crew workload.

researchUse: 2008 and 2010 International Lunar Surface Operations ISRU analogue tests (NASA, CSA, DLR, NORCAT via PISCES).
2012 RESOLVE field demonstration.

sites.name: Kīlauea Iki & Kīlauea caldera region
sites.summary: Young basaltic lava lake, flows and fumarolic deposits in Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park, used by NASA's BASALT project (2016–2017) for Mars-relevant science under simulated mission constraints.

similarities.explanation: Olivine-rich tholeiitic basalt comparable to Martian basalts analysed by Spirit in Gusev crater.
Fumarolic and steam-vent alteration deposits relevant to ancient Martian volcanic hydrothermal systems.
BASALT conducted ten simulated Mars EVAs with communication latency in 2017.
Field-portable instruments and sampling protocols tested on altered and unaltered basalt.

limitations.explanation: Earth's dense atmosphere and magnetic field shield the surface from radiation and micrometeorites; the Martian surface has neither.
Surface gravity is about 2.6 times that of Mars, which changes slope stability, sediment transport and crew workload.
Tropical rainfall and abundant vegetation nearby; biomass is much higher than any Mars analogue needs.
Humid climate rather than hyperarid.

researchUse: BASALT third field deployment (November 2017): ten simulated EVAs at Kīlauea Iki and the caldera region.

sites.name: Craters of the Moon National Monument
sites.summary: A young (2,000–15,000-year-old) basaltic volcanic field on the Snake River Plain with lava tubes, fissures and cinder cones; studied by NASA's FINESSE and BASALT teams and visited by Apollo 14 crew.

similarities.explanation: Fissure-fed basaltic volcanism similar in style to lunar mare eruptions.
Numerous accessible lava tubes and collapse pits analogous to lunar skylights.
Cinder cones and spatter ramparts along the Great Rift.
FINESSE tested handheld instruments and field-traverse concepts.
Apollo 14 astronauts trained here in 1969.
BASALT treated the area as an analogue for present-day Martian volcanic plains.
Lava tubes similar in scale to some of those inferred on Mars.
Cinder cones and spatter ramparts comparable to small scoria cones mapped on Mars.
Simulated Mars EVAs with time-delayed science support (BASALT 2016).

limitations.explanation: Earth's dense atmosphere and magnetic field shield the surface from radiation and micrometeorites; the Moon has neither.
Surface gravity is about six times that of the Moon, so suits, rovers and regolith mechanics behave differently.
Terrestrial fines lack agglutinates, nanophase iron and the sharp, unweathered grains of lunar regolith produced by space weathering.
Surface gravity is about 2.6 times that of Mars, which changes slope stability, sediment transport and crew workload.
Seasonal snow and sagebrush vegetation; soils host abundant microbes.
Lavas are less than 15,000 years old and largely unaltered, whereas many Martian volcanic surfaces are billions of years old and dust-mantled.

researchUse: FINESSE field campaigns from 2014 on lunar-style volcanism (Kings Bowl, Highway flow).

sites.name: Atacama Desert (Yungay region)
sites.summary: The hyperarid core of the Atacama, one of the driest places on Earth, whose soils are oxidising and nearly sterile; NASA's ARADS project used it to test rover-mounted drilling and life detection (2016–2019).

similarities.explanation: Rainfall of a few millimetres per year or less in the hyperarid core.
Soils contain oxidants and perchlorate that degrade organics, as at the Phoenix site.
Microbial abundance approaches the detection limit of culture-based methods.
High-altitude, cloudless conditions give some of the highest surface UV on Earth.
K-REX2 rover with a 1–2 m drill and three life-detection instruments operated remotely.
Sulfate and nitrate-rich salt crusts accumulate in the absence of rain.

limitations.explanation: Earth's dense atmosphere and magnetic field shield the surface from radiation and micrometeorites; the Martian surface has neither.
Surface gravity is about 2.6 times that of Mars, which changes slope stability, sediment transport and crew workload.
Fog and rare rain events occur; Mars has no comparable liquid-water events today.
Surface temperatures are far warmer than on Mars.

researchUse: ARADS field seasons 2016–2019 with the K-REX2 rover and life-detection payloads.
Classic studies of Mars-like soils and the dry limit of microbial life.

sites.name: Aquarius Reef Base (NEEMO)
sites.summary: An undersea habitat 19 m deep off Key Largo, where NASA's NEEMO crews live for 1–3 weeks and use weighted, tethered dives to rehearse reduced-gravity EVAs and operations with communication delays.

similarities.explanation: Ballasted divers approximate lunar-gravity mobility and EVA task loading.
Saturation diving means crews cannot surface quickly, a true isolated and confined environment.
EVA timelines, tools and sampling procedures rehearsed on the seafloor.
Reduced-gravity EVA techniques transferable to Mars (0.38 g) operations.
Used to test operations with imposed communication latency similar to Mars missions.

limitations.explanation: Water drag and buoyancy are not true reduced gravity; movement dynamics differ.
No geological analogue for lunar terrain.
Not a geological or environmental analogue for Mars.
A humid, biologically rich marine environment.

researchUse: NEEMO missions 1–23 (2001–2019), including EVA, telemedicine and latency studies.

sites.name: HI-SEAS, Mauna Loa
programs: HI-SEAS (University of Hawaiʻi; NASA Human Research Program-funded missions)
sites.summary: A habitat dome at ~2,500 m on barren lava on Mauna Loa; its long-duration isolation missions (up to one year) were funded by NASA's Human Research Program to study crew behaviour and food systems.

similarities.explanation: Four- to twelve-month isolation missions with delayed communication and suited excursions.
The habitat sits on a ~1,800-year-old basalt flow among younger flows and lava tubes.
Excursions in mock suits; limited rover use.

limitations.explanation: Earth's dense atmosphere and magnetic field shield the surface from radiation and micrometeorites; the Martian surface has neither.
Surface gravity is about 2.6 times that of Mars, which changes slope stability, sediment transport and crew workload.
Crews can be evacuated within hours; psychological isolation differs from an interplanetary mission.
Rain and fog occur; not a hyperarid environment.

researchUse: HI-SEAS missions I–V (2013–2017), funded by NASA's Human Research Program, on crew cohesion, food and sleep.

sites.name: Río Tinto (Peña de Hierro)
programs: MARTE (NASA Ames / Centro de Astrobiología, NASA ASTEP)

similarities.explanation: Jarosite, schwertmannite and other sulfates precipitate from acidic waters, as inferred at Meridiani Planum.
Iron oxides and sulfates derived from the weathering of a hydrothermal massive-sulfide deposit.

Terraced iron-rich sediments and goethite/hematite deposits.

Surface gravity is about 2.6 times that of Mars, which changes slope stability, sediment transport and crew workload.

Mediterranean climate with liquid surface water year-round.
Centuries of mining have modified the drainage chemistry.
